correctness.rationale: Williams 1977 Theorem 4 supplies exactly the local Korselt criterion on the stated coprime domain. Reducing at r-c and q-b yields k in {1,2}, j<=13 or 7, identity (jk-9)q=b(jk-3a)+kc(3-a); jk=9 is impossible, giving q<=21 and r<=65. Two exact, independent bounded sieves return six and only six signed rows, with each row satisfying all original divisibilities. CRT realizes prescribed signs with D prime congruent to 1 mod4, Dirichlet gives infinitude and the prime-number theorem in progressions gives relative density 1/8. Explicit witness discriminants passed Euler-symbol checks. None of the finite tests is used as evidence of an unbounded analytic claim.

originality.rationale: Checked Williams 1977 general criterion and constructions; 2023 preprint and expanded 2024 journal version algorithms/tabulations (including tables); related rank-based Lucas and Lucas–Carmichael literature; targeted mathematical-record searches and local prior-claim deduplication. The full six-case exact signed result across all prime discriminants and its uniform prime density were not stated or directly supplied in inspected works. General criterion is acknowledged as prior; the new output is its fully evaluated first-three-factor boundary. Unindexed equivalent computational classifications remain a risk.
residual_risks: A specialized enumeration in a source not indexed by targeted searches might give the same six rows.
The Williams criterion and newer universal enumeration algorithms make this an exact boundary evaluation rather than a fundamentally new general criterion.

value.rationale: The least prime factor 3 is the natural first boundary for a three-prime Korselt family. The theorem settles every prime discriminant simultaneously, including four mixed-sign cases beyond the classical all-positive Carmichael and all-negative Lucas–Carmichael theories. It provides an explicit exhaustive finite cutoff, a complete sign-sensitive classification of a natural family and uniform exact prime-density 1/8 per row, which supply meaningful reference cases for arithmetic prime-discriminant tabulations and tests.
